lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Hi, Mei. Before we get into tomorrow's planning, how are you doing? I saw another late platform thread last night and wanted to check on the person behind it.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I appreciate that, Priya. I'm tired, and the team is more tired than they admit in the daily check-in. We have had eleven after-hours pages in two weeks.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Eleven is a lot for three platform engineers. Is this mainly fallout from the route optimizer outage, or are we missing something about the normal support load?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Both. The outage exposed a noisy job and an alert that arrives too late, but ordinary customer escalations still land on the same three people. Nobody gets a real handoff.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: When you say no handoff, do you mean the on-call engineer keeps owning the investigation the next day too? I want to understand what part we can change now.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Exactly. They page overnight, write the fix in the morning, then sit in a roadmap meeting that afternoon. Lucas also gets pulled into ETA incidents, so the boundaries are blurry.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: That explains why the ETA model discussion keeps feeling like a capacity surprise. What have you heard directly from the team, beyond what the page count shows?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: One engineer told me they are choosing between sleep and reviewing the next deploy. Another said the on-call calendar looks fair on paper but leaves no room to recover.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: I don't want us to normalize that. Could we take one afternoon off the roadmap calendar for whoever comes off call, starting this week, and move reviews around them?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Yes, but it has to be explicit. If the afternoon is labeled free time, requests fill it. I can mark it as recovery coverage and route urgent reviews to me.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Please do that, and tell me which product reviews need another owner. I'll move those rather than ask somebody to quietly work through their recovery window.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Thank you. I also need to make the load visible. Eleven pages sounds concrete, but it misses the unpaged work, like customer data checks and incident follow-ups.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Can you put the rotation, pages, and unplanned work in one short note by Friday? I can use that in planning without turning this into a debate about anecdotes.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I can send a capacity note by Friday with the last two weeks of pages and roughly twenty-six hours of unplanned work. I'll separate verified time from estimates.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Good distinction. I don't want a precise-looking number that hides uncertainty. Is there anything we should stop this week while you gather that evidence?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: The optional platform migration review can wait. It would consume half a day and does not change customer reliability this week. I will tell the group today.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: That sounds right. I can take the cancellation message if it helps, but I want the team to hear that the decision came from capacity, not from their effort.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I would rather say it myself. They trust me to be direct. What helps is you backing the protected time when another project asks for an exception.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: You have that backing. If an exception truly cannot wait, bring it to me and we can name what moves out of the week instead of stacking it on top.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: That's the kind of tradeoff I need. I don't want another heroic week to become the baseline, and I know tomorrow's Q4 conversation could push us there again.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Let's talk about that directly. My draft for tomorrow has driver mobile v2, the ETA accuracy model, and a small self-serve onboarding pilot. None is approved yet.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I can support those as candidate bets, but only if we are honest about their different shapes. Mobile has a real delivery window; onboarding can grow without an edge.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: What would make the onboarding edge clear enough? The current average is nineteen days from signed customer to first usable dispatch, and that delay hurts us.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Start with one carrier configuration, an import template, and a human review before activation. Do not promise a general self-serve path for every carrier shape this quarter.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: That is narrower than the request Daniel brought from sales. He wants customers to sign up and move data without waiting for us. I worry a pilot disappoints them.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I hear that, but a broken import would cost more trust than a staged pilot. The platform team still owns the optimizer follow-ups and the ETA data path.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Could we quantify the choice for tomorrow instead of making it sound like product enthusiasm against engineering caution? I want the room to see a genuine tradeoff.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Yes. We have about ten usable engineering weeks after holidays and existing support work. Mobile needs four focused weeks, ETA needs three, and reliability needs two reserved weeks.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: That leaves roughly one week before onboarding. The math makes the full launch impossible, but perhaps a pilot can share some work with the import changes already planned.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Maybe, if it stays one carrier and manual review is accepted. I do not want a slide that says 'self-serve' while engineers hear 'every edge case by December.'

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Then the slide should say staged pilot, one carrier configuration, and a gate on import success and support volume. Would those terms let you advocate for it?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I could advocate for testing it. I would not commit to a broad release until we see whether the pilot reduces the nineteen-day onboarding time without increasing support tickets.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Fair. I also want to avoid counting the ETA model as done when the retraining pipeline still has quota problems. How much model work is really platform work?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: The model team owns the algorithm, but platform owns deployment, monitoring, and rollback. If the pipeline fails overnight, my people still get the page and the customer question.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: So the three weeks for ETA must include that operational slice, not just the modeling milestone. I'll make the dependency explicit in tomorrow's draft.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Please do. I would rather ask the group to cut scope in the room than leave with a plan that only works if every week is quiet.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Where would you cut first if we need another week for reliability? I know the answer might be the pilot, but I want your reasoning on the record.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I would keep the pilot's discovery and import prototype, then delay customer activation. That preserves learning while protecting mobile delivery and the ETA monitoring work.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: That is a useful fallback. I'll write it as a decision point for tomorrow, and I won't describe it as an agreed cut before the rest of the team weighs in.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Thanks. If we leave with explicit gates and a fallback, I can tell engineers the plan has limits. That matters more than an optimistic date on a slide.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: The capacity note also connects to hiring. You asked for two backend engineers. Walk me through the roles as you would explain them to Omar and the hiring panel.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: One senior backend engineer should own platform reliability and the deployment path. The second should be comfortable with carrier imports and integrations. Those are different problems.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Do we have evidence to support two separate seats rather than one generalist? Omar will ask, and I would like the answer to be sharper than 'we are busy.'

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: The on-call rotation has only three platform engineers, and the import queue is competing with incident recovery. One person cannot both stabilize the rotation and build the onboarding path.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: That makes sense. But if we get approval tomorrow, what is the realistic point at which a new hire gives the team more capacity than onboarding consumes?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Not immediately. Even with a quick process, the senior hire needs about thirty days to learn the dispatch architecture and incident history. I would not put them on a Q4 critical path.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: I appreciate you saying that. Can you write the two role briefs and a thirty-day onboarding sketch by next week? That helps us request the hires without inventing delivery capacity.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Yes. I'll draft both role briefs and the onboarding sketch by next week, with who mentors each hire and which services they can own after the first month.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: I can review them with you, then we can ask Omar about budget and sequencing. I don't want your team to feel that two approved requisitions fix this quarter's load.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: They won't. What would help now is a clear product partner when I say a bet exceeds capacity. Right now I can feel like the person who always brings the bad news.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: I have contributed to that by asking for a plan after I have already told people a date. I want you in the tradeoff discussion earlier, not just the estimation step.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I also want to grow into a director role, which means I should own more than the platform queue. I want practice making cross-team capacity choices in public.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: What part of that would stretch you usefully without simply adding another job to an overloaded week? I don't want a growth plan that reads like extra unpaid work.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Let me facilitate a monthly capacity review with leads from product, design, and data. It could replace one status meeting rather than sit on top of the calendar.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: That sounds substantive. You would frame constraints and decisions, while I support the prioritization discussion. How will you know whether it is helping your director path?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I want feedback on whether I make tradeoffs legible and whether people leave knowing what is actually funded. I also need to practice delegating technical decisions instead of rescuing them.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: I can give you feedback after the first review. For the second piece, could you choose one service review that another engineer can lead while you coach rather than drive?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Yes. I'll ask a platform engineer to lead the next optimizer review by end of week, and I'll stay available for the hard questions instead of taking the keyboard.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Let's write those as two explicit growth experiments, then review them in a month. You should have space to say if one creates more load than value.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Agreed. I want the director path to be visible, but I also want it to make the team stronger. Delegation should give them authority, not just another meeting.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: There is one piece of feedback I want to stay with. When did the last planning cycle start feeling like product handed engineering a finished answer?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: At the customer story review. The three initiatives were already on a roadmap slide, and my first invitation was to estimate them. I could change numbers, not the choices.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: I can see why that felt late. I had treated the slide as a discussion draft, but I had already repeated its dates to Daniel. That made the draft sound final.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Exactly. People can push back on a draft; they struggle when the date has already traveled. I need us to look at the problem and the capacity together first.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: For the next cycle, let's hold a joint scoping session before I circulate candidate bets. We can bring customer evidence, operational load, and rough sizing to the same table.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: That would help, as long as it produces a choice and not a longer meeting. Could we cap it at forty-five minutes and require a written list of what is deferred?

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Yes. I'll put a forty-five-minute product-engineering scoping session on the calendar next week, with one page of customer evidence and a deferred list as the output.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I'll bring the capacity note and the service ownership map. If a bet needs platform time, I want that visible before anyone quotes a launch date outside the room.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: I'll also change how I describe tomorrow's draft. I will call the three bets proposals, include the gated pilot option, and ask you to present the capacity numbers.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I can do that. Please let me explain that reliability reserves are planned work, not a contingency we can borrow whenever another milestone feels urgent.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Absolutely. I'll say that myself in the opening so you are not cast as the only voice protecting the reserve. What would make tomorrow's discussion successful for you?

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: A decision with named tradeoffs, two hiring requests treated as future support, and a clear owner for each risk. If we get that, I can make a credible plan.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: I'll revise the draft tonight and send it to you tomorrow morning for a final read. Then we can enter the room aligned on the questions, not a predetermined answer.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: And I will send the Friday capacity note, draft the hiring briefs by next week, and protect the recovery afternoon this week. Thanks for hearing the harder part, Priya.

lines.speaker: Priya Raman
lines.text: Thank you for saying it plainly. Let's check in after planning, and if the scope lands too wide, we will bring the numbers back rather than asking your team to absorb it.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: That works. I have a clearer way to explain the tradeoffs now, and I feel less alone carrying them. I'll talk to you after the planning session.
